etymology: From Latin confirmare, to make firm, from firmus, strong. Webster 1828: to make firm or more firm; to strengthen; to give new assurance of truth; to ratify. Scripture uses it of God ratifying His promise with an oath and of ministers strengthening the souls of disciples.
biblical_def: Confirm means to make firm, and Scripture applies it in three directions. Christ’s ministry confirms the promises: Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers (Romans 15:8) — the incarnation is God keeping His word to Abraham and David, and Paul makes that the ground of Gentile hope in the same passage. God confirms His counsel with an oath: men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:16-17). God swore by Himself because there was no greater, and Hebrews calls the result two immutable things — His promise and His oath — given so that believers might have a strong consolation. And ministers confirm the saints: Paul and Barnabas returned through the cities where they had just been stoned and driven out, confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Finally God confirms His people to the end: Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONFIRM as to make firm or more firm; to add strength to; to establish; to give new assurance of truth or certainty; to fix more firmly in resolution; and, in law, to ratify or make valid.
webster_full: CONFIRM, v.t. — To make firm, or more firm; to add strength to; to strengthen.
To fix more firmly; to settle or establish; as, to confirm a habit or an opinion.
To give new assurance of truth or certainty; to put past doubt; as, the news was confirmed.
To make firm or certain; to give new strength to, as an obligation; to ratify, as a covenant or a treaty.
From Latin con and firmus, strong — the root of firm, affirm, and infirmity.
scriptures: Now I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers:
For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.
Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath:
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Acts 14:22 shows what apostolic confirmation actually consisted of — the plain announcement that entry into the kingdom runs through much tribulation — which is the reverse of the encouragement most modern ministry offers.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul had just been stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and he went back through the same towns to strengthen the converts. The content of the strengthening is stated: exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God. That is not a caution appended to a cheerful message; it is the confirming word itself. Modern encouragement typically works by minimizing what lies ahead, and it fails at the first hard providence because the hearer concludes something has gone wrong. Telling a new convert the truth about the road is a kindness, and Paul evidently regarded it as the chief service he could render churches he might never see again.

Hebrews 6:17 gives the deeper ground, and it is one of the most remarkable statements in Scripture about God’s condescension. God’s bare word could not be made more certain by anything; He cannot lie. Yet willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, He swore by Himself — not because the promise needed reinforcing but because the heirs did. The oath adds nothing to God and everything to us, and the stated purpose is that we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. That is the pastoral shape of the doctrine of immutability: God stooped to the manner of men who swear, so that trembling people might rest.
roots_summary: Greek bebaioo (G950), to make firm, to confirm, to establish; bebaiosis (G951), confirmation; episterizo (G1991), to strengthen further, at Acts 14:22.
roots_lines: Greek bebaioo (G950) — to make firm, establish, confirm; Romans 15:8, 1 Corinthians 1:8, Hebrews 2:3.
Greek bebaiosis (G951) — confirmation; a legal term for the guarantee of a title (Hebrews 6:16; Philippians 1:7).
Greek episterizo (G1991) — to strengthen upon, to confirm further; Acts 14:22, 15:32, 15:41.
Greek mesiteuo (G3315) — to interpose, to confirm by mediation; God… confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:17).
Greek ametathetos (G276) — immutable, unchangeable; the immutability of his counsel in the same verse.
usage: To confirm the promises made unto the fathers (Romans 15:8) — the incarnation as God keeping His word.
Confirmed it by an oath (Hebrews 6:17) — God stooping to the manner of men who swear.
We must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22) — the content of apostolic strengthening.

etymology: From Latin possibilis, from posse, to be able. Webster 1828: that may be or exist; that may be done; not contrary to the nature of things. In the Gospels the word marks the boundary between what men can do and what God can, and Gethsemane is where our Lord Himself uses it.
biblical_def: Possible in the Gospels is used to mark a limit and then to show who stands beyond it. When the disciples asked, astonished, Who then can be saved?, the answer drew the line exactly: With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible (Mark 10:27). The context matters — the subject is not the removal of difficulties in general but the salvation of a rich man, that is, the regeneration of a heart that will not let go. Christ’s point is that conversion is a divine work and no other kind. The word appears again in Gethsemane, on His own lips: O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt (Matthew 26:39). Even there the possibility is submitted to the Father’s will, which is the pattern of every believing prayer. To the father of the epileptic boy He says, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth (Mark 9:23), and the man’s answer is one of the most honest sentences in Scripture: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. And Paul uses it with a realist’s qualification: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men (Romans 12:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines POSSIBLE as that may be or exist; that may be done; not contrary to the nature of things — and notes that possible is opposed to impossible, and is distinguished from probable, which implies likelihood.
webster_full: POSSIBLE, a. — That may be or exist; that may be now, or may come into existence.
That may be done; not contrary to the nature of things.
Possible is opposed to impossible; it is distinguished from probable, which implies not merely capacity but likelihood.
From Latin posse, to be able — whence also potent, power, and possess.
Hebrews 6:18 and Titus 1:2 mark the one class of things impossible with God: it was impossible for God to lie.
scriptures: And Jesus looking upon them saith, With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible.
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.
corruption_summary: With God all things are possible and all things are possible to him that believeth are the two most quoted and most abused sentences in the Gospels, routinely detached from the salvation they were spoken about and attached to whatever the hearer wants.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 10:27 is spoken about the salvation of a rich man and nothing else. The camel and the needle’s eye had just left the disciples exceedingly amazed, and their question was Who then can be saved? Christ’s answer is a statement about monergistic regeneration: with men it is impossible. No amount of persuasion, upbringing, or resolve produces a new heart, and the reason the rich are singled out is that wealth makes the impossibility visible. To quote the verse as a general guarantee that God will accomplish whatever a believer has set his heart on is to change its subject entirely, and it leaves the quoter with a God who has failed him as soon as the thing does not happen.

Mark 9:23 is likewise fenced by its own context. The father says if thou canst do any thing, and Christ throws the if back at him — the question is not the Lord’s ability but the man’s believing. And the response is not a triumphant profession: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief, a cry that admits faith and its deficiency in the same breath, and the boy was healed. That is the model, and it is the opposite of the teaching that a sufficient quantity of faith compels God to act. Gethsemane settles the question for good. The Son of God prayed if it be possible, and it was not possible, and He said nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. No prayer of any Christian will ever be offered from a position of greater faith than that one.
roots_summary: Greek dunatos (G1415), able, powerful, possible, from dunamai, to be able; adunatos (G102), impossible; the root of dunamis, power.
roots_lines: Greek dunatos (G1415) — able, powerful, possible; Mark 10:27, 14:35, Matthew 26:39.
Greek adunatos (G102) — unable, impossible; with men it is impossible, and it is impossible for God to lie (Hebrews 6:18).
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the root verb.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, might, miracle; from the same root, and the word behind the power of God unto salvation.
Greek ei dunaton — if possible; the exact phrase at Matthew 26:39 and Romans 12:18.
usage: With God all things are possible (Mark 10:27) — spoken about the salvation of a rich man.
If it be possible, let this cup pass from me (Matthew 26:39) — the possibility submitted to the Father’s will.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you (Romans 12:18) — peace pursued with a realist’s qualification.

etymology: From Old French enjoir, to give joy to, from joie, joy. Webster 1828: to feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession of. Scripture uses it of the pleasures of sin for a season, of God giving richly all things to enjoy, and of a land enjoying her sabbaths.
biblical_def: Enjoy in the Authorized Version is used with striking evenhandedness. Hebrews grants that sin has real pleasures and then weighs them: Moses chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:25). The pleasures were genuine, the court of Egypt was genuinely comfortable, and the decisive word is season — Moses did arithmetic, having respect unto the recompence of the reward. Against that Paul commends enjoyment in the same letter where he warns the rich: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). God is named as the giver, the giving is called rich, and the purpose is enjoyment — a sentence no ascetic reading of Scripture can absorb. Ecclesiastes says the same from the other end of a long experiment: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God (Ecclesiastes 2:24). And the word has a solemn use of the exile: then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34), the ground taking the rest Israel had refused to give it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENJOY as to feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of; and to possess with satisfaction. The possession and the pleasure in it are both included.
webster_full: ENJOY, v.t. — To feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of.
To possess with satisfaction; to occupy or have possession of, with pleasure; as, to enjoy health or an estate.
To have, possess and use with satisfaction; to have, hold or occupy, as a good or profitable thing.
ENJOYMENT, n. — The condition of enjoying; pleasure; satisfaction; fruition.
Webster’s insistence that enjoyment includes possession is useful: Leviticus 26:34 has the land enjoying sabbaths it was owed.
scriptures: Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.
Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate, and ye be in your enemies’ land; even then shall the land rest, and enjoy her sabbaths.
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
corruption_summary: Christianity is caricatured as the enemy of enjoyment, and too many Christians have earned the caricature; 1 Timothy 6:17 says God gives richly all things to enjoy, and the Westminster catechism makes enjoying Him man’s chief end.
corruption_paragraphs: The Shorter Catechism’s first answer is that man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever, and the second verb is not decoration. Paul, warning the rich in the strongest terms against highmindedness and trust in uncertain riches, grounds the warning in a positive statement about God: He giveth us richly all things to enjoy. The remedy for the misuse of good things is not their renunciation but their right use with thanksgiving, which is exactly what the same apostle says against those forbidding meats: every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. Asceticism has an appearance of wisdom, Colossians says, and no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

Hebrews 11:25 keeps the other rail in place, and it does so without pretending. Sin has pleasures. Scripture never argues that wickedness is unpleasant, which is a lie any honest person can detect, and the moment a preacher tries it he loses the young people who know better. The argument is about duration and about what is being traded: for a season, against the recompence of the reward. Moses was doing sums, not suppressing appetite. Psalm 16:11 states the alternative offer in full — fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore — and no season of Egypt’s pleasures competes with it once the terms are seen.
roots_summary: Greek apolausis (G619), enjoyment, from apolauo, to have full benefit of; Hebrew ratsah (H7521), to be pleased with or to enjoy, of the land’s sabbaths.
roots_lines: Greek apolausis (G619) — enjoyment, fruition; 1 Timothy 6:17 and Hebrews 11:25, the only two occurrences.
Greek apolauo — to have full benefit of, to enjoy; the verb behind the noun.
Greek prokairos (G4340) — for a season, temporary; the pleasures of sin for a season.
Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept, to enjoy; the land shall enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34).
Hebrew ra’ah tob — to see good, the idiom rendered enjoy good at Ecclesiastes 2:24.
usage: Than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:25) — the pleasures granted, and their term stated.
Who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17) — the ground of a warning to the rich.
Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34) — rest taken by the ground in exile.

etymology: From the Old English preposition on with sleep. Webster 1828: sleeping; in a state of sleep; at rest; and, figuratively, dead. The New Testament uses the figure for the death of believers so consistently that our word cemetery comes from the Greek for a sleeping place.
biblical_def: Asleep is the New Testament’s ordinary word for the death of a Christian, and Paul builds the doctrine of the resurrection on it. I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13) — not that believers do not sorrow, but that they do not sorrow as those who have none. The reason follows: if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him (4:14). Notice the asymmetry Paul preserves: Christ died and rose; believers sleep. He does not use the softer word of the Lord’s death, because His death was the real thing borne in full, and it is what turns ours into sleep. Paul says the same in 1 Corinthians 15: now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept (15:20). The word has an ordinary use too, and it is one of the most comforting details in the Gospels: with the ship filling and the disciples in terror, he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow (Mark 4:38). The Lord of the storm slept through it, and their question — carest thou not that we perish? — was answered by a word to the wind.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ASLEEP as sleeping, in a state of sleep; at rest; and, in Scripture, dead — noting the figurative use directly. He also gives the sense of a limb being asleep, that is, benumbed.
webster_full: ASLEEP, adv. or a. — Sleeping; in a state of sleep; at rest.
In Scripture, dead; as, concerning them which are asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
In a state of numbness; as, the limb is asleep.
The Greek koimeterion, a sleeping place, from the same verb, is the origin of the English cemetery.
The figure implies a waking, which is why Scripture never uses it of the death of the impenitent.
scriptures: But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
corruption_summary: The sleep figure has been pressed by soul-sleep advocates into a doctrine that the believer is unconscious between death and resurrection, and Scripture’s own statements about the intermediate state will not permit it.
corruption_paragraphs: Soul sleep, held by the Socinians and today by Adventists and Jehovah’s Witnesses, takes the figure literally and concludes that the dead in Christ are unconscious until the last trumpet. But Scripture is explicit about the interval. Paul is in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better — departing is immediately gain, and an unconscious sleep would not be better than fruitful labour. He tells the Corinthians that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. Our Lord told the thief, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise. Revelation shows souls under the altar crying with a loud voice. The figure of sleep describes the body, which does rest in the grave and will be raised, not the soul, which goes immediately to Christ.

What the figure does teach is worth holding tightly. It says the death of a believer is temporary, that he will be woken, and that the one who wakes him is the Lord who has already been through death Himself and emerged. Paul’s pastoral aim in 1 Thessalonians 4 is stated: that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope, and then comfort one another with these words. He does not forbid grief; Christ wept at a grave He was about to open. He forbids the hopeless kind. And Mark 4:38 gives the smaller comfort that belongs to the same doctrine — a Saviour who can sleep through a storm that terrifies experienced fishermen is a Saviour who is not alarmed by anything in a believer’s life either.
roots_summary: Greek koimao (G2837), to put to sleep, and in the passive to fall asleep or die; whence koimeterion, a sleeping place, the English cemetery; katheudo (G2518), to sleep, at Mark 4:38.
roots_lines: Greek koimao (G2837) — to fall asleep, and by figure to die; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-15, 1 Corinthians 15:20, Acts 7:60 of Stephen.
Greek katheudo (G2518) — to sleep in the ordinary sense; Mark 4:38 of Christ in the ship.
Greek koimeterion — a sleeping place, a dormitory; the early Christian name for a burial ground, whence cemetery.
Greek aparche (G536) — firstfruits; the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Greek analuo (G360) — to loose from moorings, to depart; a desire to depart, and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23).
usage: Concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not (1 Thessalonians 4:13) — grief permitted, hopelessness forbidden.
The firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20) — the resurrection guaranteed by a first instalment.
Asleep on a pillow (Mark 4:38) — the Lord of the storm untroubled by it.

etymology: From Old Norse skyrta, a shirt; the same root as shirt. Webster 1828: the lower and loose part of a coat or garment; the edge or border. In Scripture the spreading of a skirt over a woman is a formal act of covenant protection, and the cutting off of a skirt is a symbolic seizure of a kingdom.
biblical_def: The skirt is the loose lower corner or hem of a garment, and Scripture invests it with a startling amount of covenantal meaning. On the threshingfloor at midnight Ruth says to Boaz: I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman (Ruth 3:9) — not a seduction but a legal claim, the formal request that a kinsman-redeemer take her under his covering by marriage. Ezekiel turns the same act into the great allegory of God’s dealing with Jerusalem: Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine (Ezekiel 16:8). Marriage, covering, oath, covenant, possession — the whole gospel structure in one verse. The other great use is David’s in the cave: he cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily (1 Samuel 24:4), and his heart smote him afterward, because in that culture cutting the hem of a king’s robe was a symbolic taking of his authority. Haggai uses the skirt for a lesson in ritual: holy flesh carried in a skirt does not make what it touches holy, but uncleanness spreads.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SKIRT as the lower and loose part of a coat or other garment; the border, edge or margin; and the same word as shirt in origin. The border of a garment is what the Old Testament means throughout.
webster_full: SKIRT, n. — The lower and loose part of a coat or other garment; the part below the waist.
The edge of any part of dress; the border or extremity.
Border; edge; margin; extreme part; as the skirts of a town or a wood.
The word is the same in origin as shirt, from the Norse skyrta, and originally denoted simply a cut or short garment.
Numbers 15:38 commands a fringe upon the borders of the garments with a ribband of blue — the tsitsith, worn at the four corners.
scriptures: And he said, Who art thou? And she answered, I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.

Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.

And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the LORD said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily.
If one bear holy flesh in the skirt of his garment, and with his skirt do touch bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any meat, shall it be holy? And the priests answered and said, No.
The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
corruption_summary: Ruth 3 is routinely read through modern eyes as a seduction scene, which flatly reverses the narrative: it is a legal petition for redemption made by a woman of whom the whole city could say she was virtuous.
corruption_paragraphs: The threshingfloor is read as a seduction only by readers who do not know what spreading a skirt meant. The Hebrew for skirt and for wing is the same word, and Boaz had already used it of Ruth in chapter 2 — the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust. In chapter 3 she asks him to be the answer to his own blessing. His reply confirms the reading: he calls her my daughter, commends her for not following young men, says all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman, and immediately raises the legal obstacle of a nearer kinsman which he settles publicly at the gate the next morning. Naomi’s strategy was bold and it was entirely lawful, and the book was written by a people who understood the levirate law it turns on.

Ezekiel 16:8 shows what the gesture pictures, and it is the gospel. God passes by a nation that is an abandoned infant in its blood, and at the time of love spreads His skirt over her, covers her nakedness, swears, enters into covenant, and says thou becamest mine. Every element is unilateral; she contributes nothing but need. The same chapter goes on to recount her whoredoms in the most unsparing language in the prophets, and ends with God establishing His covenant with her anyway, that she may remember and be confounded and never open her mouth any more because of her shame. That is grace as Ezekiel understood it, and it is why the skirt spread over Ruth on a threshingfloor is more than a good story.
roots_summary: Hebrew kanaph (H3671), a wing, an extremity, the corner or skirt of a garment; the same word in Ruth 2:12 (wings) and 3:9 (skirt); shul (H7757), the hem or skirt of a robe.
roots_lines: Hebrew kanaph (H3671) — a wing, an edge, the corner of a garment; Ruth 3:9, Ezekiel 16:8, Haggai 2:12.
Hebrew shul (H7757) — the skirt or train of a robe; the hem of the high priest’s garment (Exodus 28:33-34), and Isaiah 6:1, his train filled the temple.
Hebrew go’el (H1350) — a kinsman-redeemer; the office Ruth invokes at 3:9.
Hebrew tsitsith (H6734) — the fringe commanded on the corners of the garment (Numbers 15:38).
The identity of wing and skirt in one Hebrew word is what ties Ruth 2:12 to Ruth 3:9 and makes the request an answered prayer.
usage: Spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman (Ruth 3:9) — a legal claim, not a seduction.
I spread my skirt over thee… and thou becamest mine (Ezekiel 16:8) — covenant grace in a single gesture.
Cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily (1 Samuel 24:4) — a symbolic seizure that smote David’s heart.

etymology: From Old English leaf. Webster 1828: one of the thin, expanded, deciduous parts of a plant; also a part of a book, and one side of a double door. Scripture opens with fig leaves sewn into aprons and closes with leaves for the healing of the nations.
biblical_def: The leaf in Scripture is a measure of a life’s condition. The first leaves in the Bible are a failed covering: after the fall, the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons (Genesis 3:7) — man’s own remedy for his shame, replaced a few verses later by coats of skins, which required a death. The psalter makes the leaf the sign of the blessed man: he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper (Psalm 1:3). Jeremiah repeats the figure with an added test: the man who trusts in the LORD shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought (Jeremiah 17:8). The point in both is the water source, not the weather. A withered leaf is Isaiah’s image of a people fading, and our Lord cursed a fig tree that had leaves and no fruit — the picture of profession without reality. And the last leaves in Scripture are healing ones: by the river of the water of life stands the tree of life, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEAF as one of the thin, expanded, deciduous parts of a plant, forming what is called the foliage; a part of a book containing two pages; and one of the two sides of a double door.
webster_full: LEAF, n., plural LEAVES — One of the thin, expanded, deciduous parts of a plant, forming what is called the foliage.
A part of a book containing two pages.
One side of a double door; also the movable side of a table.
Leaves are, in Webster’s account, the organs by which a plant takes in and gives out — which is why their state indicates the plant’s health.
The Authorized Version uses the plural leaves at Genesis 3:7, Mark 11:13, and Revelation 22:2.
scriptures: And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.

In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
corruption_summary: Psalm 1:3 is a favourite of the prosperity teachers for its closing clause, and the verse is about a root system: the leaf does not wither because of where the tree is planted, not because of what the tree resolves.
corruption_paragraphs: Whatsoever he doeth shall prosper is read as a promise of general success, and Jeremiah 17:8 shows what the promise actually covers. The tree planted by the waters shall not see when heat cometh and is not careful in the year of drought — the heat and the drought still come. What is promised is not exemption from the year of drought but a leaf that stays green in it, because the roots are spread out by the river. Psalm 1 makes the source explicit in the preceding verse: the blessed man’s delight is in the law of the LORD, and in it he meditates day and night. Prosperity in this psalm is the fruitfulness of a life fed from Scripture, and it is set against the chaff which the wind driveth away.

Genesis 3:7 and 3:21 belong together and are the whole doctrine of atonement in two verses. Adam and Eve saw their nakedness and made a covering of leaves, which is the first religion: a remedy of human manufacture, freely available, requiring no death, and entirely inadequate — they were still hiding among the trees when God came. God then made coats of skins, which He could not do without killing something. Every substitute since has been of the same two kinds. And the leaves that finally heal are not sewn by anyone; they grow on the tree of life beside the river, in a city where there is no more curse.
roots_summary: Hebrew aleh (H5929), a leaf; te’enah (H8384), the fig tree, of Genesis 3:7; Greek phullon (G5444), a leaf, at Revelation 22:2 and Mark 11:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew aleh (H5929) — a leaf, foliage; Psalm 1:3, Jeremiah 17:8, Genesis 3:7, Isaiah 64:6.
Hebrew te’enah (H8384) — the fig tree, whose broad leaves the first pair sewed together.
Hebrew kotnoth or — coats of skins; the covering God made at Genesis 3:21, requiring a death.
Greek phullon (G5444) — a leaf; Revelation 22:2, and the leaves of the barren fig tree in Mark 11:13.
Greek therapeia (G2322) — healing, service; the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
usage: They sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons (Genesis 3:7) — the first and worst covering.
His leaf also shall not wither (Psalm 1:3) — a promise about a root system, not a resolve.
The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:2) — the last leaves in Scripture.

etymology: From Old English handlian, to touch or feel with the hand, from hand. Webster 1828: to touch; to feel with the hand; to manage; to treat, as a subject. The word gives the church one of its strongest resurrection proofs and one of its sharpest warnings against man-made religion.
biblical_def: Handle in Scripture is a word of physical contact, and the New Testament uses it to settle two questions. The first is whether the risen Christ had a body. In the upper room, to disciples who were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit, He said: Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have (Luke 24:39). John opens his first epistle on the same ground: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life (1 John 1:1). Three senses are appealed to in ascending order of intimacy, and handling is the last. The second question is whether holiness consists in prohibitions. Paul quotes the ascetic slogans and dismisses them: Touch not; taste not; handle not; which all are to perish with the using; after the commandments and doctrines of men (Colossians 2:21-22). And the psalmist uses the word against the idols themselves: They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not (Psalm 115:7) — a god that cannot handle anything, worshipped by men who can.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HANDLE as to touch; to feel with the hand; to use or hold with the hand; to manage; to treat, as a subject in discourse. Both the physical and the discursive senses appear in the New Testament.
webster_full: HANDLE, v.t. — To touch; to feel with the hand; to use or hold with the hand.
To manage; to use; to wield; as, to handle a weapon or an instrument.
To treat; to discourse on; as, the preacher handled the subject with ability.
To deal with; to practise upon; as in 2 Corinthians 4:2, not handling the word of God deceitfully.
HANDLE, n. — That part of a vessel or instrument which is held in the hand; and figuratively, an occasion or advantage.
scriptures: Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life;
They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their throat.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: The bodily resurrection is the doctrine most often spiritualized, and Luke 24:39 is the verse that forecloses it: the risen Christ invited men to handle Him and ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal theology since Schleiermacher has repeatedly relocated the resurrection into the disciples’ experience — the cause of Easter faith being something that happened in them rather than to Him. Every account of that kind runs into Luke 24:39, where the disciples’ supposition that they had seen a spirit is precisely what the Lord corrects, and He corrects it by an appeal to touch and then by eating. John, writing decades later against incipient docetism, stacks the same evidence: heard, seen, looked upon, handled. Paul stakes the whole faith on it — if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain, and we are found false witnesses of God. There is no version of Christianity left if the tomb was occupied.

Colossians 2:21 addresses the opposite error, and the King James translators helpfully marked it: the slogans are the false teachers’ words, not Paul’s. Touch not; taste not; handle not is a quotation of the ascetic regime being pressed on the Colossians, and Paul’s verdict on it is severe — such things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. Rules invented by men look impressive and do nothing against sin. The remedy he gives instead is a person and a position: risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, and mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth.
roots_summary: Greek pselaphao (G5584), to feel or grope after, to handle; haptomai (G680), to touch; doloo (G1389), to adulterate, at 2 Corinthians 4:2; Hebrew mush (H4184), to feel or handle.
roots_lines: Greek pselaphao (G5584) — to handle, to feel after; Luke 24:39, 1 John 1:1, and Acts 17:27 of men groping after God.
Greek thingano (G2345) — to touch, to handle; the third verb of the ascetic slogan in Colossians 2:21.
Greek haptomai (G680) — to touch, to fasten to; the first verb of the same slogan.
Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, to corrupt as a dishonest trader waters wine; handling the word of God deceitfully.
Hebrew mush (H4184) — to feel, to handle; Psalm 115:7, and Isaac feeling Jacob’s hands in Genesis 27:12.
usage: Handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones (Luke 24:39) — the resurrection offered to touch.
Our hands have handled, of the Word of life (1 John 1:1) — an eyewitness stacking his evidence.
Touch not; taste not; handle not (Colossians 2:21) — the slogans of will worship, quoted to be refuted.

etymology: From self and same, an intensive compound meaning the very same and no other. Webster 1828: the very same; identical. The Authorized Version uses it where exactness matters — the day of the Exodus, the Spirit who distributes gifts, and the God who prepared the believer for glory.
biblical_def: Selfsame is the Authorized Version’s emphatic the very same, and it appears where the text insists on precision. The Exodus is dated to the day: at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt (Exodus 12:41). Not approximately, not in that season — the selfsame day. God keeps a calendar. Paul uses it of the distribution of gifts in the church: all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Corinthians 12:11). The diversity of gifts is real and it is not evidence of different sources or different degrees of spirituality; one Spirit apportions, and He apportions as He wills, not as the recipient chooses. And in 2 Corinthians the word carries the doctrine of glorification: having spoken of the earthly house of this tabernacle being dissolved and of the building of God eternal in the heavens, Paul writes, Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5). The believer was made for that very thing; the Spirit is the down payment; and God is the one who did the making.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SELFSAME as the very same; identical, and marks it as an intensive of same. The compound is now archaic in ordinary speech but was standard in the English of 1611 and still current in 1828.
webster_full: SELFSAME, a. — The very same; identical.
The compound is intensive: same alone might admit of a likeness, while selfsame asserts identity.
The Authorized Version uses it some fifteen times, chiefly in Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Ezekiel, and the Pauline epistles.
In the selfsame day is a legal and chronological formula in the Pentateuch (Genesis 7:13; 17:23, 26; Exodus 12:17, 41, 51).
Its persistence in modern English is almost entirely due to the King James Version.
scriptures: And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.
But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.
In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah’s wife, and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark;
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 12:11 is the verse that settles the modern quarrel about gifts, and both sides of it need the correction: the Spirit divides as he will, which rules out both the demand for a particular gift and the contempt for those who lack one.
corruption_paragraphs: The charismatic error presses believers toward a specific gift as the mark of a fuller Christianity, and Paul’s whole chapter is written against exactly that at Corinth. He asks a series of questions expecting the answer no — are all apostles? are all prophets?… do all speak with tongues? — and grounds the diversity in the Spirit’s sovereign distribution: dividing to every man severally as he will. The cessationist must hear the same verse from his side: the sovereignty asserted is the Spirit’s, not the church’s, and contempt for a member because of the gift he has or lacks is the precise sin of the foot saying it is not of the body. The chapter’s aim is that there be no schism in the body, and it ends by pointing to a more excellent way.

The chronological uses of the word deserve their own note, because they show a God who keeps dates. Noah entered the ark in the selfsame day; Abraham was circumcised in the selfsame day; Israel came out of Egypt on the selfsame day at the end of four hundred and thirty years. Paul’s when the fulness of the time was come is the same doctrine applied to the incarnation. The believer who has been waiting years for an answer is dealing with the God of the selfsame day, and 2 Corinthians 5:5 tells him what he was made for: not merely to be delivered, but to be clothed upon with a house from heaven, and the Spirit already in him is the earnest of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew etsem (H6106), a bone, and by extension the substance or self of a thing — be’etsem hayyom hazzeh, in the bone of this day, is the idiom for the selfsame day; Greek autos (G846), the same.
roots_lines: Hebrew etsem (H6106) — a bone; and figuratively the substance or very self of a thing.
Hebrew be’etsem hayyom hazzeh — literally in the bone of this day, the idiom rendered in the selfsame day.
Greek autos (G846) — self, same; one and the selfsame Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:11).
Greek arrabon (G728) — an earnest, a pledge or down payment; 2 Corinthians 5:5, Ephesians 1:14.
Greek katergazomai (G2716) — to work out, to accomplish thoroughly; he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing.
usage: Even the selfsame day… the hosts of the LORD went out (Exodus 12:41) — God keeping a four-hundred-year appointment.
That one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Corinthians 12:11) — sovereign distribution.
He that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God (2 Corinthians 5:5) — the believer made for glory.

etymology: From Latin attendere, to stretch toward, from ad and tendere, to stretch. Webster 1828: to go with or accompany; to be present at; to fix the mind upon; to listen. The Latin figure is a bow drawn toward a mark, and Scripture uses the word for the mind stretched toward instruction and toward the Lord.
biblical_def: Attend in the Authorized Version usually means to give the mind, not merely the body. Solomon’s repeated call to his son is the pattern: Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding (Proverbs 4:1), and again, My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings (Proverbs 4:20). The verb is paired with inclining the ear, keeping in the midst of the heart, and not letting them depart from the eyes — a whole discipline of retention, and it is addressed to the young because the habit is formed early or not at all. Paul uses the word once, and decisively, in his teaching on singleness: this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35). The phrase names the great advantage of the unmarried state as Paul understood it — undistracted attention — and it is offered as a liberty and not as a rule, since he has just said he speaks by permission and not by commandment. Luke uses the word of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul — the opened heart and the attending mind in one clause.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ATTEND as to go with or accompany; to be present at; to be present in business or service; to fix the mind or regard upon; to listen; to wait on. The mental sense is the biblical one.
webster_full: ATTEND, v.t. — To go with or accompany, as a companion, minister or servant.
To be present at; as, to attend a meeting or a church.
To wait on; to serve; to accompany with solicitude.
ATTEND, v.i. — To listen; to regard with attention; as, attend to the words of the wise.
From Latin ad and tendere, to stretch — attention is the mind stretched toward its object, as a bow toward a mark.
scriptures: Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know understanding.
My son, attend to my words; incline thine ear unto my sayings.
And this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction.
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Hear the right, O LORD, attend unto my cry, give ear unto my prayer, that goeth not out of feigned lips.
corruption_summary: Attention has become the scarcest commodity of the age and the most deliberately harvested, and 1 Corinthians 7:35 names undistracted attendance upon the Lord as a thing worth arranging a whole life around.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s phrase is without distraction, and he treats freedom from distraction as a real good to be weighed when a Christian considers marriage. The observation is more pointed now than when he made it, because an entire industry exists to fragment attention and is paid by the fragment. Proverbs assumes a young man capable of attending to a father’s words, inclining his ear, keeping them in the midst of his heart — sustained, retentive, unhurried attention, which is the precondition of all instruction and of all meditation. A believer who cannot hold his mind still for twenty minutes will not meditate day and night in the law of the LORD, whatever he intends. This is not a counsel of technique; it is a matter of what a man’s soul is being trained by.

Acts 16:14 keeps the doctrine straight before the discipline becomes a work. Lydia heard us, and then whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul. The hearing was hers, the attending was hers, and the opening was God’s, and Luke puts them in that order deliberately. Nobody attends savingly to the gospel by an effort of concentration. The Reformed doctrine of effectual calling is exactly this verse: the outward word preached to everyone in the riverside prayer meeting, and the Lord opening one heart to receive it. Which is why a preacher prepares his sermon with all his powers and then prays as though nothing depends on them.
roots_summary: Hebrew qashab (H7181), to prick up the ears, to attend; Greek prosecho (G4337), to hold the mind toward, at Acts 16:14; euprosedros, well-seated beside, at 1 Corinthians 7:35.
roots_lines: Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ears, to give attention; Proverbs 4:1, 4:20, Psalm 17:1.
Hebrew natah ozen — to incline the ear; the companion idiom in Proverbs 4:20.
Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold the mind toward, to give heed; Acts 16:14, 1 Timothy 4:13.
Greek aperispastos (G563) — without distraction, undivided; a hapax legomenon at 1 Corinthians 7:35.
Latin attendere — to stretch toward; whence attention, tension, and intent.
usage: Attend to know understanding (Proverbs 4:1) — the mind stretched toward instruction.
That ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction (1 Corinthians 7:35) — undistracted attention as a real good.
Whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended (Acts 16:14) — effectual calling in a single clause.

etymology: From safe, through Old French sauf, from Latin salvus, whole, unhurt — the same root as salvation. Webster 1828: in a safe manner; without incurring danger or injury; without escape or loss. In Scripture safety is always located in a Person, never in circumstances.
biblical_def: Safely in Scripture describes the condition of those God keeps, and the texts are careful to name the cause. Wisdom’s promise closes the first chapter of Proverbs: whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil (Proverbs 1:33) — and the whole chapter has been an account of the young man refusing to hearken. The psalmist ties safety to sleep, which is the body’s daily confession of dependence: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). The word only is the doctrine. God led Israel through the sea and made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies (Psalm 78:52-53). The prophets promise it of the restored people: they shall dwell safely, and none shall make them afraid. And the New Testament transposes the whole idea into a Person: Paul, awaiting execution, says I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day — safety not of the body, which was about to be killed, but of the deposit.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SAFELY as in a safe manner, without incurring danger or injury, and without escape or loss; and SAFE as free from danger, unhurt, whole. The Latin salvus underlies both safe and salvation.
webster_full: SAFELY, adv. — In a safe manner; without incurring danger or hazard of injury.
Without escape; without loss; as, the prisoner was safely kept.
SAFE, a. — Free from danger of any kind; unhurt; not lost; whole.
From Latin salvus, whole, sound, unhurt — the root of salvation, salve, and salutary.
That the English words for safety and for salvation share a root is not accidental: to be saved in Scripture is first of all to be made whole and kept.
scriptures: But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil.
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
corruption_summary: Safety has become the highest good of the age and the justification for nearly anything, while Scripture treats it as a gift located in God and freely spends the bodies of the saints.
corruption_paragraphs: The elevation of safety into a supreme value produces a religion that cannot account for the New Testament. Christ sent the twelve out as sheep in the midst of wolves and told them plainly they would be delivered up to councils and scourged; He said whoever would save his life should lose it. Paul lists his shipwrecks, stonings, and perils among his credentials. Hebrews 11 divides into those who by faith escaped the edge of the sword and those who by faith were sawn asunder, and both lists are commendations. A church that will not risk anything has quietly adopted a value the apostles did not hold, and it will find itself unable to obey ordinary commands about hospitality, evangelism, and care of the sick.

This is not a call to recklessness, which Scripture also condemns; the prudent man foreseeth the evil and hideth himself, and Paul was let down over a wall in a basket. The point is where safety is located. Proverbs 18:10 gives it exactly: the name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe — a tower, not a wall around his circumstances, and safety consisting in being inside it. Psalm 4:8 makes God the sole author, thou, LORD, only. And 2 Timothy 1:12 shows what is actually guaranteed: Paul in a Roman prison, certain of execution, persuaded that the deposit he had committed to Christ was safe against that day. His body was not safe. Nothing that mattered was in danger.
roots_summary: Hebrew betach (H983), security, confidence, safely, from batach, to trust; yasha (H3467), to save or deliver; Latin salvus behind the English.
roots_lines: Hebrew betach (H983) — security, safety, confidently; from batach, to trust or lean on.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; the root, so that to dwell safely is to dwell trustingly.
Hebrew yasha (H3467) — to save, deliver, give victory; the root of Joshua and of Jesus.
Hebrew migdal oz — a strong tower; the name of the LORD is a strong tower (Proverbs 18:10).
Greek paratheke (G3866) — a deposit committed to another’s keeping; that which I have committed unto him (2 Timothy 1:12).
usage: Whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely (Proverbs 1:33) — safety promised to the one who listens.
Thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8) — the word only carries the doctrine.
Able to keep that which I have committed unto him (2 Timothy 1:12) — a condemned man’s definition of safe.
